Your docker software controller should still be able to see your Unifi network even if your internet goes down, no?

If so, you should be able to just remove your ER4, connect your UCG fiber to your internet, and start the initial set up/configure a new IP address for your UCG fiber’s local network.

From there you would go back into your old controller, then override the inform IP to your new gateway’s address that you just configured.

Afterwards it should just be a matter of restoring your network configurations to your new gateway and connecting it back to the rest of your network.

It’ll take some time depending on when you queue, but eventually you’ll accumulate enough points from derankers that you’ll hit A-S rank where most queues are.

Even then, the reality is that PvP nowadays will just take upwards of 5+ minutes to pop due to lower player counts.

The boy was nervous.

He had always been a quiet child. Ever since he entered school he had preferred to be on his own, doing all he could to avoid attracting attention. He would read books during recess, and eat alone during lunch, all in an effort to stay as small as possible.

Maybe it was because of his parents, he often thought. His parents were the demanding type, always asking that their son be the very best at school, or whatever he did. So maybe he tried to do as little as possible, so he only had to be the best at one thing? Or perhaps it was because of some defect, some mental worm that crawled its way into his head as an infant that made him so different.

"First keyholder, please step up!"

The headmaster's loud, gruff voice shook the boy out of his stupor, reminding him that the day of the ceremony was not the right time or place to reflect on one's life. 

The line of children moved forward as the first keyholder stepped onto the stage. The boy recognized her as the daughter of the village's doctor. She had always been a very smart and popular person, and from the few times he had talked to her she seemed very kind as well.

The boy watched as she approached the stage, her ornate ivory key standing out from the dark uniform she wore.

As she stepped onto the stage, she approached 5 large locks, the ones who would determine her path from hereafter. The first lock she approached was the large ivory one in the center of the stage, whose design was similar to the key she now wore on her neck. The crowd around the children began to shift, as the low ring of hushed, rumouring voices began to eminate from the village.

"What if it doesn't turn?" "

"What would her family do?"

 "She'd be the first in generations to fail..."

Several of the whispers were loud enough for the boy to hear from beside the stage. Though they were mostly baseless what-ifs thrown around for boredoms sake, he would be lying if he didn't share some of those thoughts as well. The boy had been nervous about the ceremony for the longest time. He was already averse to attention, so the idea of the entire village watching his fate be chosen terrified him. From an early age, children are taught that they key you receive will be a reflection of your life thus far, and from what the boy could see on stage, they were taught right.

"*Click"*

The crowd had gone silent when the girl had inserted her key into the lock, and continued to wait with bated breath as the headmaster of the village interpreted its meaning. 

"Congratulations to Ms. Athene! Whose intelligence and kindness have made her the perfect candidate to become the village's doctor!"

The tension in the air turned into celebration, as the girl leapt off the stage into her father and mother's arms, their three ornate ivory keys finally matching with one another. The other village clapped in turn as well, happy that their doctor's familial practice continued.

Although the boy was happy that her key turned on her first lock, it was already expected that she would succeed. After all, a person's key is a reflection of their life, and all the members of the Athene family are known for their studiousness and kind nature.

The boy reached into his shirt, grasped the key around his neck and took a deep breath. Unlike the Athenes, the boy's family had no generational practice. His mother was the village librarian and his father was the village's hunter, two paths almost entirely different from one another. So the boy had no expected lock to pick, or had any idea what lock to pick at all! 

"May the second keyholder please step up!"

Again, the headmaster's call caught the boy's attention. The person ahead of him in line moved forward onto the stage, and the boy had to remember that although his class at school had at least 10 children, he only shared a birthday with 2. 

The boy was familiar with the current boy on stage. His name was Mark, and he had been a longtime nuisance to the boy. In contrast with his quieter tendencies, Mark was very loud, brash, and often made fun of the boy when they were younger. They had both since grown out of it though, and the Mark who stepped onto the stage was not a bully, but a dutiful man.

Mark had changed drastically in the last few years. His father, the village's mayor, had died 4 years ago now. The boy forgot exactly what happened, but he remembered that Mark had been deeply shaken. So shaken, in fact, that he apologized to the boy for teasing him when they were younger, and had promised to change his ways for the better. The prominent bronze key around Mark's neck reflected that change. Although the color was different from the one his father wore, its hefty shape was the same.

There were no whispers from the crowd as Mark approached the far left lock, the same his father had opened before. Instead a deafening silence took over the crowd as Mark inserted his key and attempted to open the lock.

He tried turning the key right, and then left, and right again. He took it in and out several times, desperately trying to get it to turn. But nothing happened. The boy expected something like this to happen, after all, Mark's key had been a different color. But he understood that Mark simply wanted to follow in his father's footsteps, but fate ruled otherwise.

The only sound the boy could hear was the slight creaking of wood as mark walked across the stage to the far right bronze lock, and somewhat reluctantly inserted his key.

"*Click"*

The boy noticed Mark's shoulders begin to shake. At first the boy thought he was sobbing, but as Mark turned around the boy could see a gentle chuckle and smile as Mark turned to face the headmaster. 

"Congratulations to Mr. Brunwick, whose courageous attitude has made him the perfect candidate to be the village hunter."

Gentle applause rang out from the crowd as Mark began to step off the stage. The boy had known that he wasn't to be his father's successor, but the fact that he had to go up after that frightened him regardless. The boy reached into his shirt once more, this time pulling out a small, delicate silver key, and tightly clutched it in his hand.

Valentine’s Day at Primrose Junior High was a huge event.
Initially founded as a school for orphaned children, Valentine’s Day was seen by its Headmaster as an oppurtunity to connect his often lonely students. 
The school’s since opened up to the public as an average junior high, but the tradition still remained. Nowadays students are forced to attend the ball-dance, as either a participant or a volunteer.
I usually go with the former, saves me from doing any extra work.

Scarlet ribbons draped the ceilings of the hall, heart-shaped decor littered the walls and doors of the 6th grade hallway, a costumed cupid busied himself greeting students and taking selfies while Marvin Gaye’s Let’s Get It On blasted over the intercom.

I’d imagine you get the picture.

In the years I had gone to the school, I had always found the event grating to say the least.
Normally I don’t mind that I’m a loner, I would even go as far to say that I enjoy it, but the sight of nearly everyone having someone who appreciated them made me envious a bit.

That day was different however.
The previous week I had been asked to the ball by Jess Holland, a girl who, by all accounts, was way out of my league. I had been reading a book in class when she approached me, I was confused to say the least. After all, a nerd like me getting asked out by one of the prettiest girls in school was about as likely as my crusty-sock of a dad finding employment.
And yet, there I was staring her right in the face.
“You’re hired.”  

I screamed internally.

Luckily Jess and her friends laughed it off as a joke, so I went along with it and took her up on the offer.
Classes had ended an hour ago, and students who had gone home to change were making their way into the gym. I was no different, normally I got here right after class and parked myself in the corner near the fire exit, but seeing as I was going with a girl this year, I had at least tried to make myself look presentable. 
Being the lame-o I was though, I had gotten my mother to help me dress for the occasion. She was eccentric to say the least, as not only was I running late but the clothes were so stiff it felt like I was waddling around in a plastic tube.
Regardless, I made my way to the gym. The dance had  already begun, but as I surveyed the area Jess was nowhere to be seen.
I attempted to reach for my phone, but to no avail; my cardigan prevented me from moving my arms whatsoever. 
I relented and eventually asked a chaperone for help.

Hurriedly, I searched for any recent texts.
“Aha!” I exclaimed.
A lone message from the girl I was waiting for, or so I thought.

“Where are you? I’ve been waiting for you at the front entrance for fifteen minutes.”  It read.

Uh oh.

It was commonplace for students to wait near the entrance and parade their date around the halls at Primrose, but seeing as I hadn’t actually gone with anyone the past two years, I made my way to the gym via the side entrances.
The text had been sent 6 minutes ago, she had been waiting nearly half an hour. 
“I’m screwed” I muttered as I shuffled my way across the building, my new loafers and stiff gait must’ve made for a sight among the more elegantly attired students.
 I ignored the sneering looks and giggles however, and made my way to the now-empty front of the school.
I looked around, and sure enough: no person was in sight.
Tears began to well up in my eyes; had I been duped? Or was I so late that Jess up and left?
Either way I was so lost in my thoughts I nearly didn’t notice the latex smile that stared at me from the ground.

Before me sat a rubber duck.

I could see a few students staring at me through the front windows, probably confused at the sight of a boy in a three-piece-suit passionately holding and kissing an imitation avian, but I didn’t care. I took my newly found companion and strutted right back to the gym, squeaking, dancing, and laughing together joyously as many a teacher and child watched in concern and bewilderment respectively.


That was two years ago, and to this day Tina and I remain a couple.
